title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Unbalanced Optimal Transport

paper.title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Unbalanced Optimal Transport
paper.abstract: Abstract Drifting models enable one-step generation by amortizing distribution transport into training, but this efficiency places greater demands on the transport field estimated at each update. In large-scale training, the field is computed from finite mini-batches of generated and real samples, which provide only imperfect approximations to the underlying distributions. Balanced optimal transport enforces exact mass matching within every mini-batch, making the estimated field sensitive to the particular composition of the real-data batch. We find that generated and real samples should be treated asymmetrically: letting the mass assigned to real samples adapt while keeping every generated sample fully transported improves generation across six feature-space metrics in controlled ablations, and is more robust to the relaxation strength than relaxing both marginals simultaneously, which falls below balanced transport under stronger relaxation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Unbalanced Optimal Transport Gradient Flow (UOT-GF), which keeps the generated-sample marginal fixed and relaxes only the real-data marginal. Under identical settings at DiT-B/2 on ImageNet-256, UOT-GF improves Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) from 1.53 to 1.46 over the balanced W-Flow baseline; scaling the same recipe yields 1.34 and 1.22 FID at L/2 and XL/2, the best FID among the one-step models we compare. We further derive the induced UOT transport force, establish a kinetic Vlasov–Fokker–Planck formulation whose overdamped zero-temperature limit recovers the drifting dynamics, and characterize non-target stationary states together with sufficient conditions for convergence.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Selected 1-NFE samples from UOT-GF-XL/2 trained from scratch on ImageNet-256 (guidance scale 1.14 1.14 ). Generative modeling seeks to transform samples from a simple reference distribution into samples from the data distribution. Diffusion and flow-based models achieve high generation quality but often require repeated network evaluations at inference time ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . GANs reduce sampling to a single forward pass, but introduce adversarial optimization and its associated training difficulties ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ; Karras et al., 2019 ) . Autoregressive and bridge-based approaches offer further alternatives, with different trade-offs between generation speed, modeling flexibility, and sample quality ( Li et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2023 ; Bortoli et al., 2021 ; Pariset et al., 2023 ) . Drifting models use a different strategy: rather than integrating a long trajectory at test time, they learn how generated particles should move toward the data distribution during training, enabling one-step sampling ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) interprets these dynamics as a Wasserstein gradient flow induced by the balanced Sinkhorn divergence and reports strong one-step performance on ImageNet-256. The practical accuracy of such a drifting update depends on how well its transport direction can be estimated during training. At each iteration, only a limited set of generated and real examples participates in the transport problem ( Han et al., 2026 ) . For large-scale datasets with substantial intra-class or local variation, the samples present in one batch need not reflect the relative prevalence of the underlying data patterns: some may be over-represented, while others may be missing altogether. ImageNet provides a representative example, where individual classes can exhibit considerable variation in appearance, pose, viewpoint, and background ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ; Tsipras et al., 2020 ) . Balanced transport still assigns a prescribed amount of mass to every sample in the batch. Consequently, the resulting coupling may be influenced by incidental batch composition ( Fatras et al., 2021 ) rather than only by the population-level structure one ultimately wishes to learn. This raises a natural question: should the generated and real samples be subject to the same marginal constraints in drifting-based training? To address this issue, we propose Unbalanced Optimal Transport Gradient Flow (UOT-GF). Unlike semi-dual, adversarial, or JKO-type uses of unbalanced transport ( Balaji et al., 2020 ; Choi et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ) , it enters as the geometry of an explicit, simulation-free drifting update, making the marginal relaxation a design axis: it defines a family of transport energies, each inducing its own flow, with balanced Sinkhorn drifting recovered as the τ → 1 \tau\rightarrow 1 member. Our central finding is that which marginal is relaxed matters : relaxing the real-data marginal alone is at least as effective as relaxing both, and is more robust to the relaxation strength—at stronger relaxation, relaxing both marginals degrades to worse than balanced transport while symmetrized source-fixed transport still improves on it. Each directed transport problem fixes its source marginal and relaxes its target marginal, and the full interaction averages contributions from both directions. Generated and real samples therefore each appear once on the fixed side and once on the relaxed side. The effective cross-interaction plan permits marginal reweighting while retaining at least half of each distribution’s reference mass, as shown in Section 3.1 . This structural property does not by itself guarantee target coverage, which we evaluate empirically in Section 5 .Our contributions are as follows: • We study marginal relaxation in gradient-flow drifting and show empirically that symmetrized source-fixed transport improves generation over balanced transport across six feature-space metrics, and is markedly more robust to the relaxation strength than relaxing both marginals, which falls below balanced transport under stronger relaxation. • We develop a unified kinetic theory connecting stochastic dynamics to deterministic drifting, with balanced Sinkhorn drifting as a special case. We establish free-energy dissipation, reveal non-target stationary states inherent to the drifting paradigm, and give sufficient conditions for reaching the target. • On ImageNet-256, relaxation improves balanced transport ( Han et al., 2026 ) at B/2 under identical settings (1.53 → \rightarrow 1.46 FID), and scaling one fixed recipe yields 1.22 FID at XL/2, a new one-step state of the art among models trained from scratch (Figure 2 ). Figure 2: Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) versus effective sampling compute (parameters × \times NFE ( Song et al., 2023 ) ) on ImageNet-256. 1-NFE samples are shown in Appendix J . sections.heading: 3 Theoretical analysis
sections.text: Several recent works have interpreted drifting models through Wasserstein gradient flows ( He et al., 2026 ; Caucheteux et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ; Dumont et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . In particular, W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) formulates drifting as the gradient flow of the balanced Sinkhorn divergence. Our method instead relaxes only the real-data marginal while keeping the generated-sample marginal fixed. Because this asymmetric transport changes both the energy and the induced force field, the existing balanced-flow analysis does not directly apply. To accommodate this setting, we first derive the transport force induced by a generalized UOT energy and show that balanced W-Flow is recovered in the hard-constraint limit (Section 3.1 ). We then develop a nonlinear Vlasov–Fokker–Planck formulation, establish free-energy dissipation, and recover the first-order drifting dynamics through overdamped and zero-temperature limits (Section 3.2 ). Finally, we analyze long-time behavior, identifying possible non-target stationary states and giving sufficient conditions for convergence to the target distribution (Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We evaluate on class-conditional ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Following W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) , a DiT-style generator operates in the SD-VAE latent space ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) , transport costs use the released pretrained MAE encoders ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , and guidance acts on the velocity with its weight sampled during training (Appendix G.4 ); sampling takes one forward pass. By default we use ten Sinkhorn iterations and ε = 0.05 \varepsilon=0.05 at every scale, since for our method ten outperform one at B/2 and L/2 (Table 3 ); W-Flow instead uses one iteration at L/2 and XL/2 and ε = 0.01 \varepsilon=0.01 at XL/2, and its other training settings are kept (Appendix G ). Ablations use DiT-B/2 for 100 epochs. FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) uses 50K samples under the ADM protocol ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ) .

sections.heading: Run-to-run variation.
sections.text: Each row of Table 1 is a single training run, so we calibrate differences against independent retrainings of the same configuration. Evaluation is deterministic given a checkpoint and sampling seed; across three sampling seeds FID varies by ± \pm 0.009. Our from-scratch retraining of the balanced baseline gives 7.07 FID and 24.21 FDr 6 at 30K steps, against 7.08 and 24.18 for the 30K checkpoint released by Han et al. (2026) under the same pipeline (they report 7.08 under their protocol). At 200K steps, our τ = 1 \tau=1 B/2 model and the released W-Flow-B checkpoint give 1.53 vs. 1.52 FID and 11.64 vs. 11.71 FDr 6 (Table 3 ). The two retrainings thus differ by 0.01 FID and 0.03 FDr 6 at 30K steps and by 0.01 FID and 0.07 FDr 6 at 200K steps, well below the differences discussed next. Over three independent training seeds, balanced and τ = 0.985 \tau=0.985 give 7.07 ± 0.05 7.07\pm 0.05 and 6.86 ± 0.06 6.86\pm 0.06 FID, and 24.21 ± 0.04 24.21\pm 0.04 and 23.54 ± 0.06 23.54\pm 0.06 FDr 6 .

sections.heading: Marginal relaxation.
sections.text: Relaxing the target marginal helps: all seven symmetrized source-fixed runs in Table 1 improve on balanced transport in FDr 6 (23.50–23.89 vs. 24.21) and in each of the six feature spaces, and so does the two-sided KL-UOT of Séjourné et al. (2019) at τ = 0.975 \tau=0.975 and 0.985 0.985 (23.97 and 23.77). Source-fixed transport is nonetheless preferable: at the respective best settings it reaches 6.86 FID and 23.54 FDr 6 against 7.00 and 23.77 for two-sided; at matched τ = 0.985 \tau=0.985 it is better in all six spaces; and it is more robust to the relaxation strength, still improving on balanced at τ = 0.95 \tau=0.95 (23.63, 6.94) where two-sided falls below it. In FID the differences are smaller and more τ \tau -sensitive for both formulations. Forward-only transport matches the symmetrized family in FDr 6 (23.81) but not in FID (7.11 vs. 6.86). Regularization ε \varepsilon also affects performance.

sections.heading: Scaling.
sections.text: The solver setting interacts with the marginal treatment: at 30K steps, balanced transport improves from one to ten Sinkhorn iterations whereas source-fixed UOT is best at one (6.72 vs. 6.86; Table 1 ); at 200K steps UOT is best at ten (Table 3 ). We therefore compare each method at its best setting. UOT-GF ( τ = 0.985 \tau=0.985 ) achieves FIDs of 1.46 / 1.34 / 1.22 \mathbf{1.46}/\mathbf{1.34}/\mathbf{1.22} at B/L/XL (Table 3 ); the XL result is a new one-step state of the art in FID among models trained from scratch. Two comparisons are controlled: at B/2, against balanced transport under identical settings (1.53; the released W-Flow-B gives 1.52), and at XL/2, where balanced transport under our recipe reaches 1.39 FID at 100K steps against 1.26 for UOT-GF with otherwise identical settings, so the gain persists at scale. The released W-Flow-L and W-Flow-XL checkpoints ( Han et al., 2026 ) (1.36/1.33) differ in solver settings (and W-Flow-XL trains 180K steps); at W-Flow’s L/2 setting (one iteration) relaxation does not help (1.40 vs. 1.36), and balanced transport at ten iterations is untested at L/2. UOT-GF remains competitive with multi-step models at substantially lower sampling compute (Figure 2 ; Figure 5 and Figure 9 ). On other feature-space metrics the picture is mixed: at B/2, where settings and guidance match, precision, recall and coverage change by less than 0.003 0.003 (Table 2 ); the lower XL recall ( 0.639 0.639 vs. 0.668 0.668 ) coincides with stronger guidance ( 1.14 1.14 vs. 1.09 1.09 ). sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced UOT-GF using symmetrized source-fixed transport, allowing marginal reweighting with lower bounds on both interaction marginals. In our experiments, it improves generation over balanced transport. Our kinetic analysis recovers drifting, including the balanced τ → 1 \tau\to 1 limit, and identifies non-target stationary states and sufficient conditions for target convergence. On ImageNet 256 256 , UOT-GF achieves a one-step state-of-the-art FID of 1.22 . These results motivate extensions to higher resolutions and broader conditional settings.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: We used large language models as writing and engineering assistants: to polish the prose and draft text from the authors’ outlines, to search for related work (every reference was checked against the original source by the authors), to help modify and debug experimental code, to typeset tables and algorithms, to check the presentation and notational consistency of the mathematical statements, and to obtain critical feedback on drafts. They were not used to generate research ideas, to design the method, to run or analyze experiments, or to produce any reported result or figure. All content produced with their assistance was reviewed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the paper.

sections.heading: Appendix A Notation
sections.text:

sections.heading: Optimal transport and its relaxations.
sections.text: Optimal transport lifts a ground cost on samples to a geometry on distributions ( Villani, 2009b ; Santambrogio, 2015 ; Peyré and Cuturi, 2019 ) . Entropic regularization makes it tractable via Sinkhorn iterations ( Cuturi, 2013 ) and improves sample complexity from the curse-of-dimensionality rate of plain OT to a parametric rate ( Genevay et al., 2018a ; Mena and Niles-Weed, 2019 ) ; the entropic bias is removed by the Sinkhorn divergence, which is positive, definite, and metrizes weak convergence ( Genevay et al., 2018b ; Feydy et al., 2018 ) . Unbalanced OT replaces the hard marginal constraints by Csiszár penalties, allowing mass to be created or destroyed ( Liero et al., 2015 ; Chizat et al., 2016 ) , and Séjourné et al. (2019) extend Sinkhorn divergences to this setting, proving positivity for symmetric penalties. In the mini-batch regime, balanced OT is known to produce couplings that the population plan would never form, and unbalanced mini-batch OT was proposed as the remedy ( Fatras et al., 2020 ; Fatras et al., 2021 ) . Our energy is a source-fixed member of the unbalanced family, debiased so that the target is stationary (Section 3.1 ).

sections.heading: Wasserstein gradient flows.
sections.text: Gradient flows of energy functionals in the Wasserstein geometry originate in the JKO scheme and Otto calculus ( Jordan et al., 1998 ; Otto, 2001 ) , with the metric-space theory of Ambrosio et al. (2005) ; see Santambrogio (2017) for an overview. In machine learning they have been instantiated with kernel discrepancies ( Arbel et al., 2019 ; Mroueh and Nguyen, 2021 ; Glaser et al., 2021 ; Hertrich et al., 2024 ) , variational and discriminator-based divergences ( Gao et al., 2019 ; Ansari et al., 2021 ; Fan et al., 2022b ) , JKO steps parameterized by input-convex networks ( Mokrov et al., 2021 ; Alvarez-Melis et al., 2022 ; Bunne et al., 2022 ) , and unbalanced transport with an inner adversarial solve ( Choi et al., 2024 ) . These methods integrate the flow at inference time or through a costly inner optimization; drifting models instead amortize it into the generator’s training trajectory. Kinetic lifts of Wasserstein flows and their overdamped limits are classical in PDE theory ( Villani, 2009a ) and have been studied as accelerated sampling schemes ( Ma et al., 2019 ) ; we use them to place drifting inside a Langevin-type hierarchy (Section 3.2 ).

sections.heading: Optimal transport in generative modeling.
sections.text: The Wasserstein distance entered generative modeling as a GAN critic ( Arjovsky et al., 2017 ; Gulrajani et al., 2017 ; Salimans et al., 2018 ) and as a Sinkhorn-divergence loss ( Genevay et al., 2018b ) . A second line learns the transport map itself, through input-convex potentials ( Makkuva et al., 2020 ; Korotin et al., 2021 ) or neural dual solvers ( Korotin et al., 2023 ; Rout et al., 2022 ; Fan et al., 2022a ) . Unbalanced transport was introduced for robustness to outliers via robust OT ( Balaji et al., 2020 ) , machine unlearning generative models ( Choi et al., 2026 ) and semi-dual UOT maps ( Choi et al., 2023 ) ; these rely on adversarial or semi-dual formulations and have been demonstrated up to CelebA-HQ. OT couplings also straighten flow-matching paths ( Tong et al., 2024 ; Pooladian et al., 2023 ) and underlie Schrödinger-bridge samplers ( Bortoli et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) . We use unbalanced transport differently: not as a loss to be minimized by an inner solver, but as the geometry that defines the velocity of an explicit drifting update.

sections.heading: Drifting models and their interpretation.
sections.text: Drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) train a one-step generator by regressing each sample onto a stop-gradient target displaced along a kernel-based attraction–repulsion field, reaching 1.54 FID on ImageNet-256. Several works have since interpreted the field. With Gaussian kernels it is a difference of kernel-density score estimates, connecting drifting to score matching and to Wasserstein flows of smoothed divergences ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ) ; Franz et al. (2026) show the original field is not conservative, and Caucheteux et al. (2026) give a unifying variational account of generative Wasserstein flows. Finite-particle rates for conservative and non-conservative fields are established by Balasubramanian (2026) . On the algorithmic side, He et al. (2026) replace one-sided kernel normalization by Sinkhorn coupling, restoring identifiability; W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) realizes drifting as the Wasserstein gradient flow of the balanced Sinkhorn divergence with a convergence guarantee for the particle dynamics and state-of-the-art one-step results; Esteban-Casadevall et al. (2026) use kernel gradients, Zhang et al. (2026a) regress onto multi-step drifts, Dumont et al. (2026) constrain the dynamics to transport maps, and Feng et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026b) match distributions in representation space. Drifting has also been applied to speech enhancement, medical imaging, and policy optimization ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Zhang, 2026 ) . All of these inherit balanced transport, or a kernel surrogate of it, as the geometry of the field; to our knowledge, our work is the first to relax its marginal constraints, showing that a source-fixed unbalanced geometry improves on it under identical settings on ImageNet.

sections.heading: One-step generation.
sections.text: Beyond drifting, one-step generators are obtained by distilling multi-step models ( Song et al., 2023 ; Lu and Song, 2025 ; Frans et al., 2025 ) , by learning average velocities ( Geng et al., 2025 ) , or adversarially ( Karras et al., 2019 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Drifting-type methods differ in requiring neither a teacher nor a discriminator.

sections.heading: ImageNet experiments.
sections.text: Detailed hyperparameters and configurations are given in Table 5 . We largely follow the setup of W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) without extensive hyperparameter tuning; the only new hyperparameters are the marginal penalties ( φ 1 , φ 2 ) (\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2}) , the relaxation strength τ \tau , and the symmetrization of the velocity estimator. Experiments are conducted on Nvidia H20 GPUs with 141 GB of memory each. The B/2, L/2, and XL/2 models are trained on 8 nodes of 8 GPUs; the ablations use a single node of 8 GPUs. Training L/2 takes about 5 days.

sections.heading: G.2 Source-Fixed Sinkhorn Solver
sections.text: For a cost matrix 𝐂 ∈ ℝ N × M \mathbf{C}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times M} with uniform weights 1 N ​ 𝟏 N \tfrac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N} , 1 M ​ 𝟏 M \tfrac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M} , the source-fixed problem equation 12 with ( φ 1 , φ 2 ) = ( ι , KL ) (\varphi_{1},\varphi_{2})=(\iota,\mathrm{KL}) is solved in the log domain. With 𝐊 := − 𝐂 / ε \mathbf{K}:=-\mathbf{C}/\varepsilon and τ = ρ / ( ρ + ε ) \tau=\rho/(\rho+\varepsilon) , initialize log ⁡ 𝐛 = 𝟎 \log\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{0} and iterate L L times log a i ← log 1 N − LSE j ( K i ​ j + log b j ) , log b j ← log 1 M − τ LSE i ( K i ​ j + log a i ) , \log a_{i}\leftarrow\log\tfrac{1}{N}-\operatorname{LSE}_{j}\big(K_{ij}+\log b_{j}\big),\qquad\log b_{j}\leftarrow\log\tfrac{1}{M}-\tau\operatorname{LSE}_{i}\big(K_{ij}+\log a_{i}\big), (118) where LSE is log-sum-exp. The first update is the exact source projection ( φ 1 = ι \varphi_{1}=\iota ); the second is the KL-relaxed target projection, whose exponent τ < 1 \tau<1 is the standard damping for a ρ ​ KL \rho\,\mathrm{KL} penalty ( Séjourné et al., 2019 ) . After the loop one further source update is applied so that the returned plan P i ​ j = exp ⁡ ( log ⁡ a i + K i ​ j + log ⁡ b j ) P_{ij}=\exp(\log a_{i}+K_{ij}+\log b_{j}) satisfies 𝐏𝟏 M = 1 N ​ 𝟏 N \mathbf{P}\mathbf{1}_{M}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N} exactly for any finite L L ; this also keeps the particle velocities correctly scaled. Setting τ = 1 \tau=1 recovers balanced Sinkhorn and hence W-Flow.

sections.heading: Effective interaction and marginal bounds.
sections.text: Define the effective cross-interaction matrix 𝐏 ¯ := 1 2 ​ ( 𝐏 → + ( 𝐏 ← ) ⊤ ) . \overline{\mathbf{P}}:=\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\mathbf{P}^{\to}+(\mathbf{P}^{\leftarrow})^{\top}\big). The estimator can equivalently be written as Velocity ​ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) i = N ​ ∑ j P ¯ i ​ j ​ ( 𝐲 j − 𝐱 i ) . \text{{Velocity}}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})_{i}=N\sum_{j}\overline{P}_{ij}(\mathbf{y}_{j}-\mathbf{x}_{i}). Since each directed solve fixes its source marginal, 𝐏 → ​ 𝟏 M = 1 N ​ 𝟏 N , 𝐏 ← ​ 𝟏 N = 1 M ​ 𝟏 M . \mathbf{P}^{\to}\mathbf{1}_{M}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N},\qquad\mathbf{P}^{\leftarrow}\mathbf{1}_{N}=\tfrac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M}. Consequently, 𝐏 ¯ ​ 𝟏 M \displaystyle\overline{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{1}_{M} = 1 2 ​ ( 1 N ​ 𝟏 N + ( 𝐏 ← ) ⊤ ​ 𝟏 M ) ≥ 1 2 ​ N ​ 𝟏 N , \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Big(\tfrac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}+(\mathbf{P}^{\leftarrow})^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{M}\Big)\geq\tfrac{1}{2N}\mathbf{1}_{N}, (121) 𝐏 ¯ ⊤ ​ 𝟏 N \displaystyle\overline{\mathbf{P}}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{N} = 1 2 ​ ( ( 𝐏 → ) ⊤ ​ 𝟏 N + 1 M ​ 𝟏 M ) ≥ 1 2 ​ M ​ 𝟏 M , \displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\Big((\mathbf{P}^{\to})^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{N}+\tfrac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M}\Big)\geq\tfrac{1}{2M}\mathbf{1}_{M}, (122) where the inequalities are componentwise. Equivalently, the associated measure π ¯ = ∑ i , j P ¯ i ​ j ​ δ ( 𝐱 i , 𝐲 j ) \bar{\pi}=\sum_{i,j}\overline{P}_{ij}\delta_{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{j})} satisfies π ¯ 1 ≥ 1 2 ​ q ^ , π ¯ 2 ≥ 1 2 ​ p ^ . \bar{\pi}_{1}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\widehat{q},\qquad\bar{\pi}_{2}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\widehat{p}. Thus, the effective cross interaction allows marginal reweighting while retaining at least half of each reference marginal. These bounds also hold for finitely many Sinkhorn iterations, up to floating-point error, because both directed solves end with a source projection. They concern cross-interaction mass and guarantee neither a nonzero net force nor target coverage.

sections.heading: Symmetry of the construction.
sections.text: For the symmetric cost and common regularization parameters used here, transposing a transport plan gives UOT ϕ 1 , ϕ 2 ​ ( q , p ) = UOT ϕ 2 , ϕ 1 ​ ( p , q ) . \mathrm{UOT}^{\phi_{1},\phi_{2}}(q,p)=\mathrm{UOT}^{\phi_{2},\phi_{1}}(p,q). Exchanging the two marginal penalties therefore leaves the symmetrized cost A A , the energy E p E_{p} , and its exact gradient field unchanged. Here “source-fixed” describes each directed solve; the full construction uses symmetrized one-sided relaxation. This symmetry concerns the exact transport objectives, whereas the marginal bounds above also apply to the finite-iteration plans.

sections.heading: G.4 Guidance
sections.text: Following Han et al. (2026) , the guidance weight w w is sampled at each training step from the distribution in Table 5 and the generator is conditioned on it, so a single model covers w ∈ [ 0 , 3 ] w\in[0,3] ; at inference a fixed w w is chosen by search and sampling remains one forward pass. We report guidance as s := w + 1 s:=w+1 in the main text. For a class 𝖼 \mathsf{c} and weight w w , three velocities are estimated from the same generated batch: 𝐯 ^ 𝖼 \widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathsf{c}} toward real samples of class 𝖼 \mathsf{c} , 𝐯 ^ self \widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{self}} toward a second generated batch of class 𝖼 \mathsf{c} , and 𝐯 ^ ∅ \widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing} toward N unc N_{\mathrm{unc}} real samples drawn from all classes. The regression target uses 𝐯 ^ w = ( 𝐯 ^ c − 𝐯 ^ self ) + w ⁡ ( 𝐯 ^ c − 𝐯 ^ ∅ ) , \widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{w}=(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{c}-\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathrm{self}})+w\,(\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{c}-\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing}), (123) in which the self-interaction term cancels from the guidance difference. No label dropout is used; the unconditional direction comes from the unconditional data batch, not from an unconditional generator.

sections.heading: G.5 Feature-Space Transport
sections.text: Costs are squared Euclidean distances between features of the released pretrained MAE encoder ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , C i ​ j ℓ = 1 2 ​ ‖ ψ ℓ ​ ( 𝐱 i ) − ψ ℓ ​ ( 𝐲 j ) ‖ 2 C^{\ell}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}\|\psi_{\ell}(\mathbf{x}_{i})-\psi_{\ell}(\mathbf{y}_{j})\|^{2} , computed independently for each selected block ℓ \ell . Plans, velocities, and the regression target are formed per block, and the per-block losses are averaged. Block selection and feature normalization follow Han et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: Synthetic transport diagnostics.
sections.text: We construct four two-dimensional source–target problems to compare balanced OT with symmetrized source-fixed UOT under target perturbations. Let { 𝐱 i } i = 1 N \{\mathbf{x}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} and { 𝐲 j } j = 1 M \{\mathbf{y}_{j}\}_{j=1}^{M} denote the source and target samples with uniform weights 1 N ​ 𝟏 N \tfrac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N} and 1 M ​ 𝟏 M \tfrac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M} . In every experiment the ground cost is C i ​ j = 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 i − 𝐲 j ‖ 2 C_{ij}=\tfrac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{y}_{j}\|^{2} and the entropic regularization is ε = 0.05 \varepsilon=0.05 . The balanced baseline minimizes ⟨ 𝐂 , 𝐏 ⟩ + ε KL ( 𝐏 ∥ 1 N ​ M 𝟏 N 𝟏 M ⊤ ) subject to 𝐏𝟏 M = 1 N 𝟏 N , 𝐏 ⊤ 𝟏 N = 1 M 𝟏 M . \langle\mathbf{C},\mathbf{P}\rangle+\varepsilon\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathbf{P}\,\big\|\,\tfrac{1}{NM}\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{M}^{\!\top}\big)\quad\text{subject to}\quad\mathbf{P}\mathbf{1}_{M}=\tfrac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N},\qquad\mathbf{P}^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}_{N}=\tfrac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M}. The source-fixed unbalanced variant instead solves min 𝐏 ≥ 0 , 𝐏𝟏 M = 1 N ​ 𝟏 N ⟨ 𝐂 , 𝐏 ⟩ + ε KL ( 𝐏 ∥ 1 N ​ M 𝟏 N 𝟏 M ⊤ ) + ρ KL ( 𝐏 ⊤ 𝟏 N ∥ 1 M 𝟏 M ) , \min_{\mathbf{P}\geq 0,\;\mathbf{P}\mathbf{1}_{M}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N}}\langle\mathbf{C},\mathbf{P}\rangle+\varepsilon\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathbf{P}\,\big\|\,\tfrac{1}{NM}\mathbf{1}_{N}\mathbf{1}_{M}^{\!\top}\big)+\rho\,\mathrm{KL}\big(\mathbf{P}^{\!\top}\mathbf{1}_{N}\,\big\|\,\tfrac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M}\big), where τ = ρ / ( ρ + ε ) = 0.985 \tau=\rho/(\rho+\varepsilon)=0.985 , corresponding to ρ ≈ 3.283 \rho\approx 3.283 . The displayed optimization problems define one directed solve. We solve each problem in both directions, obtaining 𝐏 → ∈ ℝ + N × M \mathbf{P}^{\to}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N\times M} for source-to-target transport and 𝐏 ← ∈ ℝ + M × N \mathbf{P}^{\leftarrow}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{M\times N} for target-to-source transport, with the cost matrix transposed and the reference weights exchanged in the reverse solve. The effective cross-interaction plan is 𝐏 ¯ := 1 2 ​ ( 𝐏 → + ( 𝐏 ← ) ⊤ ) . \overline{\mathbf{P}}:=\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(\mathbf{P}^{\to}+(\mathbf{P}^{\leftarrow})^{\top}\bigr). For source-fixed UOT, 𝐏 → ​ 𝟏 M = 1 N ​ 𝟏 N \mathbf{P}^{\to}\mathbf{1}_{M}=\frac{1}{N}\mathbf{1}_{N} and 𝐏 ← ​ 𝟏 N = 1 M ​ 𝟏 M \mathbf{P}^{\leftarrow}\mathbf{1}_{N}=\frac{1}{M}\mathbf{1}_{M} . Consequently, 𝐏 ¯ ​ 𝟏 M ≥ 1 2 ​ N ​ 𝟏 N , 𝐏 ¯ ⊤ ​ 𝟏 N ≥ 1 2 ​ M ​ 𝟏 M , \overline{\mathbf{P}}\mathbf{1}_{M}\geq\frac{1}{2N}\mathbf{1}_{N},\qquad\overline{\mathbf{P}}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{N}\geq\frac{1}{2M}\mathbf{1}_{M}, componentwise. Thus, each directed solve fixes its own source marginal, while both effective marginals may be reweighted. The balanced comparison uses τ = 1 \tau=1 in both directions. The plans are computed with Algorithm 2 in double precision; the balanced baseline sets τ = 1 \tau=1 , and no diagonal mask is applied. The four problems use L = 3000 / 80 L=3000/80 , 3000 / 150 3000/150 , 400 / 400 400/400 , and 3000 / 80 3000/80 iterations for the balanced/source-fixed solvers, respectively. All random samples are reproducible from the base seed 20260831, with separate deterministic seed offsets for each source, target, and perturbation.

sections.heading: Wrong-manifold replacement (Figure 7 ).
sections.text: We sample 192 source points and 120 clean target points from a five-arm pinwheel. sections.heading: Efficiency evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluated all methods at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution on NVIDIA H20 GPUs, assigning one GPU to each process. Inference used FP32 tensors with TF32 enabled. We retained each model’s high-fidelity sampling configuration: SiT-XL/2 used a 250-step Euler SDE sampler with CFG 1.5 1.5 and the official EMA VAE; RAE-XL used a 50-step Euler ODE sampler with autoguidance 1.42 1.42 ; BAR-L used guidance 5.3 5.3 , temperature 3.0 3.0 , token allocation [ 2 , 2 , 5 , 7 ] [2,2,5,7] , and KV caching; and UOT-GF used its 200k-step XL checkpoint with CFG 1.14 1.14 and one generator evaluation. For throughput, we used a batch size of 125, discarded 10 warm-up batches, and timed the following 390 batches. Throughput is the number of timed images divided by the elapsed generation-and-decoding time. For single-image latency, we fixed the conditioning label to ImageNet class 0, discarded 20 warm-up requests, and timed 200 batch-one requests individually, synchronizing CUDA immediately before and after each request. We report the mean latency; checkpoint loading and file I/O are excluded from both timing measurements. We estimated FLOPs per image by running the complete sampling and decoding path under PyTorch’s FlopCounterMode and dividing the counted operations by the batch size. These are theoretical estimates for supported operators, not measurements of hardware utilization or energy consumption. The speedup in panel is each model’s batch-125 throughput divided by SiT-XL/2’s batch-125 throughput. Figure 9: Single-H20 inference efficiency at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution. (c) Mean batch-one generation-and-decoding latency over 200 timed requests. (d) Batch-125 throughput speedup relative to SiT-XL/2. Both panels use logarithmic vertical axes and model-specific high-fidelity sampling settings. The speedup in (d) is not computed from batch-one latency.

sections.heading: Controlled visualization of target-marginal relaxation.
sections.text: Figure 10 isolates the transport mechanism by applying balanced OT and source-fixed UOT to the same generated sources and real ImageNet targets. The 128 source particles are generated with a fixed seed from our frozen EMA W-Flow-XL/2 checkpoint at 180k steps (class 178, CFG 1.14). The 128 targets consist of 96 distinct class-178 images, 16 exact copies of four of those images, and 16 foreign-class images (class 0). We encode the targets as 4096-dimensional global SD-VAE latents and use the training-time input scaling and quadratic cost for both operators, with ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 ( ϵ eff = 204.8 \epsilon_{\mathrm{eff}}=204.8 ) and 10 Sinkhorn iterations; source-fixed UOT additionally uses τ = 0.985 \tau=0.985 . Only the positive-forward coupling is shown. The upper plots report each target’s received mass relative to its uniform reference mass: balanced OT keeps this ratio near one, whereas source-fixed UOT preserves the source marginal while allowing target-specific deviations through a soft KL penalty. The lower heatmaps show row-normalized coupling density relative to uniform, with target columns grouped into clean images, duplicate families, and foreign-class images. This controlled probe visualizes marginal adaptation, rather than comparing separately trained generators or establishing a difference in image quality. sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our analysis establishes force identities, kinetic lifting, and stationary-state examples under the stated assumptions. Positive definiteness is known for symmetric generators under the conditions of Séjourné et al. (2019) , but remains open for the source-fixed energy, as do the trajectory assumptions required for convergence. The convergence statements concern the population flow; the mini-batch update with finitely many Sinkhorn iterations is the next object to analyze. Empirically, why the mild forward-plan reweighting observed on ImageNet (Figure 6 ) improves generation remains open, and the controlled comparison with balanced transport is at B/2; L/2 and XL/2 are system-level results with a fixed transport recipe. Experiments are on ImageNet-256 in the SD-VAE latent space with DiT generators; other datasets and latent spaces remain to be explored.

sections.heading: Broader impact.
sections.text: One-step generation produces an image in a single forward pass, making high-quality synthesis cheaper to serve, easier to embed in interactive settings, and less energy-intensive at inference than diffusion and flow models. It carries the familiar hazards of generative imagery: fabricated or misleading content, reproduction of training-data stereotypes, and likenesses generated without consent. Our method adds one consideration: marginal reweighting may affect the representation of underrepresented samples, and aggregate precision and recall do not establish subgroup coverage, so subgroup-level evaluation remains necessary. We support standard release practices: content provenance or watermarking, documented training data and intended use, and access controls or output filtering outside research contexts.

Affiliation: Ant Group Junpeng Jing Affiliation: Imperial College London Lu Gan Affiliation: Brunel University of London Cong Ling Affiliation: Imperial College London Abstract Drifting models enable one-step generation by amortizing distribution transport into training, but this efficiency places greater demands on the transport field estimated at each update. In large-scale training, the field is computed from finite mini-batches of generated and real samples, which provide only imperfect approximations to the underlying distributions. Balanced optimal transport enforces exact mass matching within every mini-batch, making the estimated field sensitive to the particular composition of the real-data batch. We find that generated and real samples should be treated asymmetrically: letting the mass assigned to real samples adapt while keeping every generated sample fully transported improves generation across six feature-space metrics in controlled ablations, and is more robust to the relaxation strength than relaxing both marginals simultaneously, which falls below balanced transport under stronger relaxation. Motivated by this observation, we propose Unbalanced Optimal Transport Gradient Flow (UOT-GF), which keeps the generated-sample marginal fixed and relaxes only the real-data marginal. Under identical settings at DiT-B/2 on ImageNet-256, UOT-GF improves Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) from 1.53 to 1.46 over the balanced W-Flow baseline; scaling the same recipe yields 1.34 and 1.22 FID at L/2 and XL/2, the best FID among the one-step models we compare. We further derive the induced UOT transport force, establish a kinetic Vlasov–Fokker–Planck formulation whose overdamped zero-temperature limit recovers the drifting dynamics, and characterize non-target stationary states together with sufficient conditions for convergence. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Selected 1-NFE samples from UOT-GF-XL/2 trained from scratch on ImageNet-256 (guidance scale 1.14 1.14 ). Generative modeling seeks to transform samples from a simple reference distribution into samples from the data distribution. Diffusion and flow-based models achieve high generation quality but often require repeated network evaluations at inference time ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . GANs reduce sampling to a single forward pass, but introduce adversarial optimization and its associated training difficulties ( Goodfellow et al., 2014 ; Karras et al., 2019 ) . Autoregressive and bridge-based approaches offer further alternatives, with different trade-offs between generation speed, modeling flexibility, and sample quality ( Li et al., 2024 ; Tian et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2023 ; Bortoli et al., 2021 ; Pariset et al., 2023 ) . Drifting models use a different strategy: rather than integrating a long trajectory at test time, they learn how generated particles should move toward the data distribution during training, enabling one-step sampling ( Deng et al., 2026 ) . W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) interprets these dynamics as a Wasserstein gradient flow induced by the balanced Sinkhorn divergence and reports strong one-step performance on ImageNet-256. The practical accuracy of such a drifting update depends on how well its transport direction can be estimated during training. At each iteration, only a limited set of generated and real examples participates in the transport problem ( Han et al., 2026 ) . For large-scale datasets with substantial intra-class or local variation, the samples present in one batch need not reflect the relative prevalence of the underlying data patterns: some may be over-represented, while others may be missing altogether. ImageNet provides a representative example, where individual classes can exhibit considerable variation in appearance, pose, viewpoint, and background ( Deng et al., 2009 ; Russakovsky et al., 2015 ; Tsipras et al., 2020 ) . Balanced transport still assigns a prescribed amount of mass to every sample in the batch. Consequently, the resulting coupling may be influenced by incidental batch composition ( Fatras et al., 2021 ) rather than only by the population-level structure one ultimately wishes to learn. This raises a natural question: should the generated and real samples be subject to the same marginal constraints in drifting-based training? To address this issue, we propose Unbalanced Optimal Transport Gradient Flow (UOT-GF). Unlike semi-dual, adversarial, or JKO-type uses of unbalanced transport ( Balaji et al., 2020 ; Choi et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2024 ) , it enters as the geometry of an explicit, simulation-free drifting update, making the marginal relaxation a design axis: it defines a family of transport energies, each inducing its own flow, with balanced Sinkhorn drifting recovered as the τ → 1 	auightarrow 1 member. Our central finding is that which marginal is relaxed matters : relaxing the real-data marginal alone is at least as effective as relaxing both, and is more robust to the relaxation strength—at stronger relaxation, relaxing both marginals degrades to worse than balanced transport while symmetrized source-fixed transport still improves on it. Each directed transport problem fixes its source marginal and relaxes its target marginal, and the full interaction averages contributions from both directions. Generated and real samples therefore each appear once on the fixed side and once on the relaxed side. The effective cross-interaction plan permits marginal reweighting while retaining at least half of each distribution’s reference mass, as shown in Section 3.1 . This structural property does not by itself guarantee target coverage, which we evaluate empirically in Section 5 .Our contributions are as follows: • We study marginal relaxation in gradient-flow drifting and show empirically that symmetrized source-fixed transport improves generation over balanced transport across six feature-space metrics, and is markedly more robust to the relaxation strength than relaxing both marginals, which falls below balanced transport under stronger relaxation. • We develop a unified kinetic theory connecting stochastic dynamics to deterministic drifting, with balanced Sinkhorn drifting as a special case. We establish free-energy dissipation, reveal non-target stationary states inherent to the drifting paradigm, and give sufficient conditions for reaching the target. • On ImageNet-256, relaxation improves balanced transport ( Han et al., 2026 ) at B/2 under identical settings (1.53 → ightarrow 1.46 FID), and scaling one fixed recipe yields 1.22 FID at XL/2, a new one-step state of the art among models trained from scratch (Figure 2 ). This is the field we generalize: Section 3.1 replaces the balanced energy by an unbalanced one and derives the resulting force, and Section 3.2 recovers the mean-field dynamics underlying equation 3 as the overdamped, zero-temperature limit of a kinetic lifting. 3 Theoretical analysis Several recent works have interpreted drifting models through Wasserstein gradient flows ( He et al., 2026 ; Caucheteux et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ; Gretton et al., 2026 ; Dumont et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2026 ) . In particular, W-Flow ( Han et al., 2026 ) formulates drifting as the gradient flow of the balanced Sinkhorn divergence. Our method instead relaxes only the real-data marginal while keeping the generated-sample marginal fixed. Because this asymmetric transport changes both the energy and the induced force field, the existing balanced-flow analysis does not directly apply. To accommodate this setting, we first derive the transport force induced by a generalized UOT energy and show that balanced W-Flow is recovered in the hard-constraint limit (Section 3.1 ). We then develop a nonlinear Vlasov–Fokker–Planck formulation, establish free-energy dissipation, and recover the first-order drifting dynamics through overdamped and zero-temperature limits (Section 3.2 ). Finally, we analyze long-time behavior, identifying possible non-target stationary states and giving sufficient conditions for convergence to the target distribution (Section 3.3 ). 3.1 UOT–Sinkhorn Energy and Its First Variation Let p , q ∈ 𝒫 ⁡ ( Ω ) p,q\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega) , Ω ⊂ ℝ d \Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} , and c ⁡ ( 𝐱 , 𝐲 ) = 1 2 ​ ‖ 𝐱 − 𝐲 ‖ 2 c(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=	frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{y}\|^{2} .
